title: What is a class loader, and what are the types (Bootstrap, Extension/Platform, System/Application, Custom)?
shortTitle: What is a class loader and what are the types?

s1_definition.profdef: A class loader is a part of the JVM responsible for finding the bytecode for a class and loading it into memory on demand, producing a `Class` object. Java uses a hierarchy of class loaders: the Bootstrap class loader loads the core platform classes, the Platform class loader (called Extension before Java 9) loads additional platform modules, and the System or Application class loader loads classes from the application classpath. Developers can also write Custom class loaders to load classes from unusual sources such as a database, a network, or an encrypted archive.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of class loaders as the librarians at National Bank of India's code library. When the transfer program first mentions an Account class, a librarian must fetch the Account blueprint from the shelves and bring it into the working room. There are different librarians for different shelves: one senior librarian only handles the most trusted core books that came with the building (Bootstrap), another handles the official extensions, and the everyday librarian fetches the bank's own application books like TransferService. If the bank keeps some blueprints in a locked vault or downloads them over the network, it hires a custom librarian who knows how to fetch from those special places.
s1_definition.oneliner: A class loader finds and loads class bytecode on demand, and Java layers them as Bootstrap, Platform, Application, and optional Custom loaders.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A class loader is a part of the JVM responsible for finding the bytecode for a class and loading it into memory on demand, producing a `Class` object. Java uses a hierarchy of class loaders: the Bootstrap class loader loads the core platform classes, the Platform class loader (called Extension before Java 9) loads additional platform modules, and the System or Application class loader loads classes from the application classpath. Developers can also write Custom class loaders to load classes from unusual sources such as a database, a network, or an encrypted archive.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of class loaders as the librarians at National Bank of India's code library. When the transfer program first mentions an Account class, a librarian must fetch the Account blueprint from the shelves and bring it into the working room. There are different librarians for different shelves: one senior librarian only handles the most trusted core books that came with the building (Bootstrap), another handles the official extensions, and the everyday librarian fetches the bank's own application books like TransferService. If the bank keeps some blueprints in a locked vault or downloads them over the network, it hires a custom librarian who knows how to fetch from those special places.

**One line to remember:** A class loader finds and loads class bytecode on demand, and Java layers them as Bootstrap, Platform, Application, and optional Custom loaders.

sections.s2_technical:
Classes in Java are loaded lazily, meaning the JVM loads a class the first time it is actually needed, not all at once at startup. The class loader's job is to locate the compiled bytecode, read it, verify it, and define a `Class` object that the JVM can use. You can see which loader loaded a class by calling `getClass().getClassLoader()`; for a core type like String it returns null because the Bootstrap loader is represented as null.

The Bootstrap class loader is the top of the hierarchy. It is written in native code, not Java, and loads the core runtime classes such as those in java.lang and java.util. Because it is native, it is represented as null when you query it. It is the most trusted loader and loads the classes the whole platform depends on.

The Platform class loader, known as the Extension class loader before Java 9, loads additional platform-level classes and modules that are part of the JDK but not the innermost core. The System or Application class loader loads the classes of your own application from the classpath or module path. This is the loader that loads your TransferService and Account classes, and it is the one returned by `ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader()`.

A Custom class loader is one you write by extending `ClassLoader` and overriding `findClass`, where you supply the raw bytes and call `defineClass` to turn them into a Class. For example a bank might load plugin rule classes from an encrypted file or a remote server. Custom loaders power application servers, hot redeployment, and plugin systems. A senior nuance is that two classes with the same name loaded by two different loaders are considered different types by the JVM, which is a common source of ClassCastException in complex deployments, and that custom loaders must be written carefully to respect the delegation model so they do not accidentally reload core classes.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to load fraud-detection rules as plugins that can be updated without restarting the main service. The core application classes like Account come from the normal application classpath, but the rule classes live in a separate folder that compliance updates frequently. This is exactly what class loaders enable, because the standard Application loader handles the core classes while a separate loader can bring in the plugin rule classes from the special folder.

Problem 2 — The team needs to understand which loader loaded which class, so they can reason about isolation. When they print the loader of String versus the loader of Account, they see that core classes report a null loader (Bootstrap) and application classes report the Application loader. This is exactly the loader hierarchy in action, and observing it makes the layering concrete.

In the mini-project we build a small inspector plus a custom loader concept. We define an `Account`, a `FraudRule` interface, and a `RuleInspector` that prints the class loader for several classes. The demo prints the loader of java.lang.String (Bootstrap, shown as null), the loader of the application's Account class (Application loader), and the system class loader itself, so we can clearly see the three standard layers at work in a banking context.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a request to inspect the class loaders of java.lang.String and the application's Account class, created for Rajesh (SAV2001).

Step 1: When the JVM first ran this program it loaded the core classes it needs, like String, using the Bootstrap loader. Because Bootstrap is native code, the JVM represents it as null. So when we call getClassLoader on a String instance, the result is null.

Step 2: The program created an Account for Rajesh. The first time Account was referenced, the Application class loader found Account.class on the classpath, verified it, and defined the Class. So calling getClassLoader on the Account instance returns the Application loader, not null.

Step 3: RuleInspector.reportLoader runs for String. It reads the loader, sees null, and logs that String was loaded by Bootstrap, shown as null. This proves core classes sit at the top of the hierarchy.

Step 4: RuleInspector.reportLoader runs for Account. It reads the loader, sees the Application loader, and logs its name. This proves our own classes are loaded by the Application loader.

Step 5: The program walks the parent chain from the system loader upward. The Application loader's parent is the Platform loader, and the Platform loader's parent is Bootstrap, shown as null. This visualizes all the layers at once.

```text
[INFO] java.lang.String loaded by: Bootstrap (native, shown as null)
[INFO] com.bank.loader.Account loaded by: jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@...
[INFO] System (Application) loader: jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@...
[INFO]   its parent (Platform) loader: jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@...
[INFO]   Platform's parent (Bootstrap): null
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  First reference to a class triggers loading
    │
    ▼
  Which loader owns it?
    │
    ├─ java.lang.String  ──▶ Bootstrap loader (native) → reported as null
    ├─ jdk platform types ─▶ Platform loader
    └─ com.bank.* classes ─▶ Application/System loader (classpath)
                               (optional) Custom loader → DB/network/encrypted jar

  Parent chain (child asks parent first):
    Application ──parent──▶ Platform ──parent──▶ Bootstrap(null)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  Fraud Service (JVM)         │
  │  ──────────────────────────  │
  │  AppClassLoader:             │  loads Account, FraudService (core app)
  │     └─ loads core app classes│
  │  CustomRuleLoader (extends    │  loads FraudRule plugins from:
  │     ClassLoader):            │     - /rules/*.class  (hot folder)
  │     └─ defineClass(bytes)     │     - encrypted jar / remote URL
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
                  │ reads plugin bytes
         ┌────────┴─────────┐
         ▼                  ▼
  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │ rules/ folder│   │ remote store │
  └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘
  Compliance updates rules without restarting the core service.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — ClassLoader hierarchy ═══

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │     <<abstract>> ClassLoader │
  │  + loadClass(name): Class    │  delegates to parent first
  │  # findClass(name): Class    │  override point for custom
  │  # defineClass(bytes): Class │  bytes → Class object
  │  + getParent(): ClassLoader  │
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
      extends      │
   ┌───────────────┼───────────────────────────┐
   ▼               ▼                            ▼
  Bootstrap    PlatformClassLoader       AppClassLoader
  (native,     (jdk modules)             (classpath: Account, Service)
   null)                                        │ parent
                                          CustomRuleLoader (your plugins)

  ── Call Chain (first reference to Account) ──
  1. new Account(...) triggers load
  2. AppClassLoader.loadClass("...Account")
  3.   → delegate to Platform.loadClass → Bootstrap (not found there)
  4.   → AppClassLoader.findClass reads Account.class from classpath
  5.   → defineClass(bytes) → Class<Account>
  6. instance created

  Note: same class name + two loaders = two DIFFERENT types to the JVM.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A class loader is the part of the JVM responsible for finding the compiled bytecode of a class, reading and verifying it, and turning it into a Class object in memory. Classes are loaded lazily, meaning the first time a class is actually referenced, so the class loader is what brings a type to life on demand rather than everything being loaded at startup.

Java organizes class loaders into a hierarchy with distinct responsibilities. At the top is the Bootstrap class loader, which is written in native code and loads the core platform classes like those in java.lang and java.util. Because it is native, the JVM represents it as null, which is why calling getClassLoader on a String returns null. Below it is the Platform class loader, which was called the Extension class loader before Java 9, and it loads additional platform modules that ship with the JDK but are not the innermost core.

Next is the System or Application class loader, which loads my own application's classes from the classpath or module path, so my TransferService and Account are loaded by this one, and it is the loader returned by getSystemClassLoader. Finally there are Custom class loaders, which I can write by extending ClassLoader and overriding findClass to supply raw bytes to defineClass. Custom loaders let me load classes from unusual sources like an encrypted jar, a database, or a remote server, and they are what power application servers, plugin systems, and hot redeployment.

In my banking work the practical use is loading fraud-detection rules as plugins that compliance can update without restarting the core service, where the Application loader handles the core classes and a custom loader brings in the rule classes from a hot folder. One senior nuance I always mention is that two classes with the same name loaded by two different loaders are treated as completely different types by the JVM, which is a classic cause of ClassCastException in complex deployments, so custom loaders must be written to respect the delegation model. So my complete answer is that a class loader lazily finds and loads class bytecode, and Java layers them as Bootstrap for core classes, Platform for JDK modules, Application for my own classes, and optional Custom loaders for special sources.

---

keyPoints: Class loader: loads .class bytecode into JVM memory at runtime
Bootstrap: loads core Java (java.lang, java.util) — written in native code
Application: loads your application classes from classpath
Custom class loaders: application servers, plugin systems, hot reload
